[h1] An absolute legend. Timeless. Immortal. [/h1]

I’ve played this game for years, and honestly, no matter how many modern shooters come and go, CS 1.6 still stands tall. This isn’t just a game — it’s a piece of gaming history.

No flashy skins, no hand-holding, no nonsense. Pure skill, pure aim, pure adrenaline. Every clutch mattered. Every footstep made your heart race. LAN cafés, late nights, endless Dust2 matches, shouting “rush B” like it was a life philosophy — unforgettable memories.

The gunplay is crisp, movement is unforgiving, and the skill ceiling is brutally high. You don’t win because of loadouts or perks — you win because you’re better. Simple as that.

Even today, it teaches fundamentals that most modern FPS games can’t. Crosshair placement, recoil control, teamwork — CS 1.6 built legends.

If you’ve played it, you already know.
If you haven’t, you missed something special.

A true GOAT. Forever respected. 🐐

I really wanted to like CS2. I gave it so many chances, played for hours, telling myself “okay, maybe this time it’ll be better,” but honestly, the more I played, the more tired I got. Throughout all the time I’ve spent in the game, there are just way too many cheaters, and it’s become seriously frustrating. After a while, you just lose all motivation.

You join a match and at first everything feels normal. Then a few rounds in, something feels off. Someone keeps one-tapping you through walls, never misses, always knows exactly where you are. You tell yourself, “Maybe they’re just really good,” but by the end of the match, you realize it’s not about skill at all.

What annoys me the most is this: you actually put in effort. You practice your aim, you try to improve your game sense, but someone else can wipe out all that effort with a single cheat. It really kills your enthusiasm. Even when you win, it doesn’t feel satisfying anymore.

CS2 isn’t a bad game. It has a lot of potential. The graphics, the gunplay, the overall feel of the game are actually good. But if the cheating problem keeps going like this, no matter how good the game is, it just pushes people away. At some point, you start asking yourself, “Why am I playing a game just to get angry?”

In short, I want to love CS2, but the game isn’t giving me the same energy back. I don’t want to leave matches feeling stressed and annoyed instead of having fun. :(

This game has gone through some wild shifts and changes over the years, and it is a battle royale first and foremost above all others, so if that is not your vibe, steer clear. 

That said, for a free to play adaptation from a pay to play core, PUBG has thrived since it's initial ups and downs of finding a good foothold in a market that quickly got overtaken by flashier and more cartoony competitors.  

This is a great game to just casually knock out a few drops with some friends or goof off in solo que doing self imposed absurd challenges, and the casual mode doubly makes it much less of a chance of just getting completely stomped by people who eat sleep and breath the game while your just trying to play with people of varying skill level and interest in the game. 

As it stands now, it is a solid free to play BR option for the people who prefer less cartoony asthetics with more realistic style firearms. It certainly is not a full hardcore vibe on the realistic feel so won't really scratch the itch there, but overall it has a lot going for it in it's specific niche.  The competitive scene is also quite impressive and for such a random variable element of a game that often comes down to luck over skill in terms of equipment strategies, it is still very entertaining to watch in spite of the inherent lack of a certain degree of mechanical balance optimization just due to the nature of the game itself. 

There are also very amusing custom lobbies that can be tweaked into all kinds of improvised game modes for very silly group fun if your lucky enough to be part of a community that can muster the numbers to host such a thing! 

The journey of improvement and refinement is a constant one that never truly ends however, and these are the things I think could do with some changes to improve the quality of the game and extend it's reach even further: 

[b] CASUAL REWORKS [/b] 

Change casual ques to 90min instead of 60min and allow groups who are queing together to go off the time remaining of the group member with the most time remaining, even if other group members have 0 time remaining themselves. people meet up and decide to do a little casual play at different points in the day, in different circles, this helps make this process not feel like a time triage excercise similar to scheduling DnD groups 

[b] BOT DROP [/b]

Adding a purely co-op comp stomp mode would be very helpful for those of us who enjoy playing casuals but do not want the human competitive element in any way beyond friendly team competition to see who can get the most kills / coolest kills. 

Someone like me can go toe to toe easily in the main matches and the "who's a bot and who's not" excitement of casuals is something I can handle easily enough, but for a lot of people I play with who enjoy a purely casual against bots experience that is not high pressure so they can be comfortable and spend time with friends and loved ones without getting upset or too overly stressed, something like this would be much better: 

The maps are much smaller environments (they can just be zoomed in sections of already existing maps to start with, but eventually custom designed maps using pre-existing assets would be the best course of action to help with differentation at a glance and variety) 

The game mode would be 100 participants, with up to 6 six slots occupied by players in one team replacing a bot spawn from either a pre-que or public lobby (with players still able to launch on less than max numbers) 

Everyone parachutes in at the same time in random spots in the sky above the map and have to steer themselves into locations alongside all the bots, and then it's just a free for all as the bots do not have teams, but they always priortize engaging human players over one another (and are generally coded to miss each other as much as possible when fighting one another) they will never kill downed players intentionally, and as the match progresses and the circle tightens, the bots become universally stronger, more well equipped, and deadlier, all while ensuring their top priority is to avoid the closing circle, up to the point of not stopping to engage until they are inside of it at all costs (and also reducing outside of circle damage to the bots so a ton of them don't just die out there like in casuals) 

I could elaborate a great deal on more specifics and unique elements of this game mode, but this review only has so much room so if the devs would like to contact me directly, I would happily provide additional expansion and development plans to streamline it's inception!

[b] FAT TRIMMING [/b] 

 There is soooo much overlapping emergency key jingling from this games years of desperate reinvention and expansion that needs cleaning up. There are so many absurd sub menus and six different currencies doing the same things that could all be solved by one that make the monetized elements far more complex and annoying to engage with. 

Making a "give me all my stuff I qualify for" button that just lists a history of where and why a thing was given to the player is so much more effective and gives people a less micro management heavy way of cleanly aquiring things. It should also store and log those qualified rewards until that button IS clicked even if the event or whatever was going on has passed, so that people don't accidentally miss out on things they qualified for simply because of an arbitrary timer. 

In addition, make the actual BP shop it's own thing that makes it easier to navigate what is available purely with BP without mixing it with the premium currency shop. You can still put advertisements in the BP shop items directing too premium shop versions, and you can add a premium shop currency buy options for all the BP items too even, but make the designation more clear, and simple to navigate 

Again, I have a massive list of UI reconfigurations and changes to offer in great detail, along with many mechanic revisions and refinements, if the developers are interested. I understand the limitations of development especially on a skeleton crewed F2P investment anchor, but I know how to work on nothing budgets with little resources, so happy to offer my expertise if desired! 

[b] NO MORE SOLO DANCES [/b] 

This one is mildly irksome, but ALL dances of every kind should be group dances. This is a nitpick I will admit it, but it's just unnecissarily exclusionary in a largely team incentivizing game. Add a toggle when activating the dance for it to be solo only if you really want to keep that for more mean spirited players, but don't enforce exclusion. 

I could go on an on and on about ideas for new events, tweaks and optimizations, promotional tie ins and baseline improvements but, again, due to limited space here, I'll just end on saying this game is not perfect by far, and it will be infuriating at times both because of the PVP nature of the game, and some of the games baked in elements at it's core, but if you want a slower paced BR That has less frenetic energy than other BR's and Arena Shooters while still being an engaging experience with a bit more of a "real life" influence, this one is the game for you! And it's free, and there are random little events that pop up free game modes to play with so, it's worth keeping installed just to mess around with now and then!

[h1]“A Stylish PvPvE Extraction Shooter With Real Tension”[/h1]

Arc Raiders is a sci‑fi extraction shooter set on a ruined future Earth, where you head topside from the underground hub of Speranza to scavenge, fight, and (hopefully) extract alive. It mixes PvE against brutal ARC machines with PvP against other Raiders, and the whole loop is built around risk, teamwork, and smart decision‑making. When a run goes well, it feels incredible; when it goes wrong, you know exactly why.

[hr]

[h1]What makes it great[/h1]

[b]⚡ High‑stakes extraction gameplay[/b]
• Every trip to the surface is a gamble: how long you stay and how much you carry is entirely your call.
• If you die before extracting, you lose what you brought and what you found.
• Successful extractions feel earned, especially after surviving multiple encounters in a row.

[b]🤖 Fighting ARC and other Raiders[/b]
• ARC machines range from drones to towering walkers, each with distinct attack patterns.
• PvPvE means you’re never just fighting AI—other players can ambush you, third‑party fights, or steal your loot.
• Deciding when to engage, when to hide, and when to run is a constant, satisfying tension.

[b]🧭 Speranza and long‑term progression[/b]
• Speranza acts as your safe hub: pick contracts, manage gear, and plan your next run.
• Upgrading weapons and equipment gives clear, tangible progression without turning the game into pure stat grind.
• Better gear opens up riskier routes and more aggressive playstyles.

[b]🎨 Strong identity and atmosphere[/b]
• The retro‑futuristic aesthetic and ruined‑Earth landscapes give the game a distinct look.
• Sound design sells the danger—ARC movements, distant gunfire, and extraction ships all add to the tension.
• The world feels hostile but readable once you learn its rhythms.

[hr]

[h1]Early rough edges[/h1]

• Solo play is possible, but the game clearly shines in squads.
• Match quality can vary depending on how many coordinated teams are in your lobby.
• Some weapons and builds feel stronger than others and will likely see balance passes.

[hr]

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

Arc Raiders is a tense, stylish PvPvE extraction shooter where every decision—what you bring, where you go, when you extract—actually matters. If you enjoy high‑risk looter‑shooters where survival depends on awareness, teamwork, and good judgment, this is absolutely worth your time.

This is the first time i've written a review on this platform. I've played many video games, and over the last 3-4 years i hadn't found anything that felt truly fun. I've played a lot of very good games during that time, but none like this one-specially in that sense.

I'm going to tell a story, and while I don't think it's a particularly unique Raider story, it is unique to me, and really sums up how I feel about the game.

It was my last run, and I noticed and event was going on, something like "The Blue Gate" or whatever. I'd had a pretty good night, so I figured I'd hop in and see what it was. I wasn't really expecting anything, honestly I didn't really know where the gate even was.

I asked several people, and eventually discovered where the gate was (FYI, it's the giant gate on the map labeled "Gate:). I mozey on over, and eventually bump into someone explaining the gate to someone else. I follow them until I eventually find a large group in a control tower (8-12 ish people) strategizing on who's going to get the last keys. Meanwhile, a guy was in the corner complaining about how he already got a key and never gets to go in because he's always finding codes when it's opened (he'll become important later). 

They come up with a strategy and leave. I have no idea what's going on, but they're labeled on the control panel, so I tell the dude complaining to grab a beer, and that I'll go grab one. I assumed I was following them up the hill, but when I get up there, I'm all alone... and I don't know what a key looks like or where to find one. Assuming it works like all other keys in the game, I start cracking shit open. It takes a while, but eventually I found it! Dodging ARC patrols, I make my way down the hill, but apparently I had taken too long, because when I got back, the dude that was complaining said the whole group had gone up to the top to find the key. 

I asked "Well, should we do it?" and he said "Uhmm... yeah." I smashed that key in with my whole face, and we went to war.

And by we, I mean more him, for unknown to me, there's a bastion in there (the guys before only mentioned the loot). Complaining dude just goes "I got it, need the damage anyways," and unloads some kind of rocket launcher on it while a couple other dudes join up. We poke it down, clean up, and sing goop until the nukes come in.

There's a certain level of measured chaos that's required to make games good. I think a good deal of that chaos has been removed from games because designing spectacle is a herculean, both from a creative prospective (vision) and from a design prospective (logistics). Introducing any element that could lead to chaos is not only a technical nightmare, but really runs the risk of not being received well and detracting from your vision, maybe even destroying it.

ARC nails this, and stories like the one above seem to be run of them mill, if that experience is the kind you like (looking at you, sweats). 

There's a lot more great things going on here too. Economic balancing is never going to be perfect, but their heads are in the right place, and they're doing better than anyways else so far. Systems that are meant to be punishing feel fair and balanced. Missions are great to. Items feel amazing as well. Gunplay is great. Sound needs to be dialed in, but mostly because it's so good that it's easy to spot when it's not quite working right. 

The only thing I really want at this point is more. I've got plenty of road ahead of me. Looking at their development plan, it seems like there will be plenty more new road once this one runs out, and even if there's not, they've already got a plan for that too.

I expected this game to be a little bit like Warframe, where you walk around a safe hub, craft gear, experiment with your build by mixing and matching the various components, and cooperate with teammates to finish quests and get out alive. In reality, this game has a narrow-minded poorly thought out philosophy of gameplay. Here are the main gripes I have with ARC Raiders:

- There is no way to test loadouts and weapons safely. You cannot experiment with loadouts or specific weapons to see how they handle unless you are ok with running the risk of losing them. We are therefore disincentivized from building a skill set and crafting an identity.

- There is no obvious way to use text chat. On top of being a valuable fallback option for team communication, text chat could also offer a way to log information to the squad without having to repeat oneself over voice chat. Unfortunately, the narrow-minded design philosophy of the developer renders them incapable of even conceiving that text chat might offer valuable and meaningful utility. The fact that the game has existed for several months without a staple like text chat should make it clear that this developer is not worth wasting time on.

- Controls do not automatically remap to accommodate for alternative keyboard layouts. This is not a very serious problem since all controls can be remapped manually, albeit with no way to tell what bindings controls had before they were overwritten. Still, auto remapping is an industry standard. Refusal to follow this standard could potentially be a sign of sloppiness under the hood, so I thought I would include this gripe here.

- There is no way to sync up quests. How many more of an item does my teammate need to complete a quest? How do I show my teammates how many more items I need? I was unable to find a way to relay this information. This just compounds the profound frustration around being unable to communicate basic information. This is another problem that no competent developer would ever allow to see the light of day. It also segues into my final gripe...

- There is no way to divvy up the loot in a safe environment. Say you have just returned from a bountiful journey with squad mates. Surely there must be a way to swap the loot you each found while on your journey, all from the safety of the local bar or an apartment? Does my teammate need one last of a certain item that I found in surplus during our journey? Astonishingly, there is no way whatsoever to do any post-game loot swapping.  This is yet another industry standard that somehow managed to slip the mind of the developer. You actually have to bring the loot back up to the surface just to exchange it. That's like having to go to the international space station just to split some chicken nuggets from McDonald's.

If I were the developer, I would be way too embarrassed even to provide the canned response that they probably use to answer reviews like this, let alone provide an actually thought-out defense, which would be borderline impossible. It's a damn shame too. This game could have been great if it hadn't been dragged down by what I can only assume is developer complacency.

I bought Rust thinking it would just be another survival game I’d mess around in for a weekend. I’d seen clips of raids, roof camping, and funny naked players running around with rocks, and I figured: “Yeah, I’ll try it out. Looks chaotic but fun.”

That was one of the worst decisions I’ve ever made.

At first, Rust felt amazing. The tension of hearing footsteps outside your base, the fear when a helicopter flies overhead, the rush of finding your first gun — it was all addictive in a way I didn’t fully understand yet. I told myself I’d just play a couple hours… then suddenly it was 3 AM. Then 5 AM. Then the sun was coming up and I hadn’t slept.

Fast forward to 70+ hours, and I realized something terrifying: Rust didn’t just become a game I played — it became my entire life.

I stopped caring about other games. I stopped caring about my normal routine. I’d sit at my PC thinking about Rust even when I wasn’t playing. “Should I move my base?” “Did my doors decay?” “What if someone is raiding me right now?” I’d be lying in bed stressing about pixels in a video game like it was real life.

The thing about Rust is that it messes with your brain. You don’t just play it — you live in it. Every scrap matters. Every minute matters. Every decision feels high stakes. If you log off for too long, you might wake up to your base completely wiped and everything gone. That fear alone keeps you glued to your screen longer than any game ever should.

Socially, Rust also destroyed me for a bit. I stopped talking to friends as much. I skipped calls. I ignored messages because I was “busy defending base.” I’d tell people, “Yeah, I’ll hop off soon,” and then not log off for another four hours. My sleep schedule got absolutely cooked. I started staying up way too late, grinding for loot that would probably just get raided anyway.

And that’s the cruel joke of Rust — no matter how hard you work, you can lose everything overnight. You can spend 10 hours building a base, farming, crafting guns, grinding components… and then some sweaty clan comes along at 3 AM and blows it all up while you’re offline. All that effort? Gone. For nothing.

But here’s the worst part: even after all that, I still wanted to keep playing. Rust is rage-inducing, stressful, and sometimes downright miserable… yet it’s also insanely compelling. The highs are ridiculously high. Winning a big raid, surviving a crazy fight, or outsmarting other players feels better than almost any other game I’ve played.

So did Rust ruin my life? In a way… yeah. At least for a while. It turned me into a sleep-deprived grinder who cared way too much about a virtual base. It made me angry, paranoid, and obsessed. I lost track of time constantly.

But was it also one of the most memorable gaming experiences I’ve ever had? Also yes.

Rust isn’t just a game — it’s a psychological experiment disguised as a survival sandbox. If you value your time, your sleep, or your sanity… do not buy this game. But if you’re curious, reckless, and want to experience pure chaos, betrayal, adrenaline, and stress in digital form… welcome to Rust. You’ve been warned.

Rust is not a game. It’s a long-term psychological condition. You don’t start playing Rust — you slowly disappear from real life and nobody notices because you’re “just busy this wipe.”

You spawn naked, afraid, and hopeful. This is the last time you’ll feel hope. Within minutes, a man who hasn’t seen the sun since Obama was president kills you with military-grade hardware and screams something illegal into voice chat. This becomes normal.

I skipped three Christmases with my family. Not because I was busy. Because there was a wipe. While normal people ate dinner and exchanged gifts, I was sitting in a dark room, listening for footsteps, heart rate at 140, guarding virtual doors that no longer exist.

I played 19 hours a day. Sleep was a suggestion. Food was optional. Hydration was replaced with Mountain Dew until my body started sending error messages. Rust didn’t just simulate survival — it tried to kill me in real life. Immersion 10/10.

The progression system is genius. You farm for days so someone else can take everything in 10 minutes while you’re offline experiencing something meaningless like “human connection.” Base building isn’t content — it’s charity.

The community is the final boss. Children screaming. Adults roleplaying war crimes. “Friendly” players betraying you before your crafting menu closes. Voice chat feels like a leaked audio file from a court case.

Eventually, my graphics card burned out. Literally died. The only thing that saved me.
I went outside for the first time in years. It was winter. I wore sunglasses. Not for style — my eyes weren’t calibrated for daylight anymore. I flinched at footsteps. I checked corners. Rust followed me home.

And yet… I miss it.
Every kill felt illegal.
Every death felt personal.
Every wipe felt like a chance to finally be happy (it wasn’t).

Recommended
For players who:

don’t need a social life

think trauma builds character

hear footsteps in silence

10/10 — lost time, sanity, relationships, a GPU, and part of my soul.
See you next wipe.

[h1] TLWR: Wide as the ocean, deep as a puddle. Bad writing. Fun to be had but wait for a deep discount. [/h1] 

Bad writing, Main story puts you in control of three pretty loathsome characters making it difficult to really root for any of them. This also goes for any side characters in both single player and online, aside from a very select few, most are very annoying. Which is disappointing because GTA has always been very good at creating if not characters you can root for, then characters that are at least enjoyable. The main story also tries (and fails) to make a point at sometimes, but then immediately re-negs on said point. For example: [spoiler] There is a mission where you need to torture/interrogate someone suspected to be a terrorist; there entire time two characters are going on about how 'torture tactics never work and someone will pretty much say anything you want for you to stop torturing them, leading to false positives. But throw that all out of the window because after all of that blabbing. It works! You get the right guy.[/spoiler] Most of the story is almost a carbon copy of the movie 'Heat' as well. They did that for GTAIV as well but it was really only just a handful of missions, not the whole damned game. I honestly think no-one working on this game played GTAIV or any of the earlier games and I think that is pretty evident in some of the opening missions, like when [spoiler] Johnny from GTA Lost and the Damned gets killed in the games opening act. In a very uncharacteristic way might I add. I hated Johnny in Lost and the Damned but even then, having him be a strung out meth head in a trailer park goes so far against his character in GTA IV that it's almost a fucking insult. Johnny hated meth, didn't want to sling it and saw it ruin people very close to him. It was kind of a huge part of that games story. [/spoiler] - not a huge deal but emphasizes my point in that these writers were hacks. 

Speaking of hacks! On we go to GTA Online:

While I like that there are certainly plenty for you to do in both single player and online, none of the distractions really seem to go anywhere. Within about 20, 30 minutes you're just recycling the same missions. 

Most of the fun to be had in this game is in GTA Online, however it's not really worth it. It really all depends on how much you like busy work, how much you're willing to deal with being grieved, and if you have likeable friends to play with. The phrase "but it's fun with friends..." isn't enough to save a game. Literally everything is more fun with friends.  The game punishes you for doing well, as well; If you earn too much money at one given time, it just wont give it to you which is just peachy. Especially if you're a 'Rockstar VIP' more often than not, your second spin of the daily casino wheel will get poached out of your hands because of this. 

Graphics are nice and hold up I guess, but Rockstar always makes humans look as ugly as possible. That, and graphics just aren't enough to prove a game is good. 

Controller support isn't great. Sometimes it will just shut off your controller mid mission, awesome. Especially with newly added content. There are also some pretty game breaking glitches. For instance: In GTA online there is a (very overused) mission type where you deliver goods by van, anytime you hit the brakes the back of the van lifts as tied to a string and you are pretty much helpless as you dangle in your van and get shot at. Bunkers are bonkers: a 15-minute supply run window feels unnecessarily restrictive and turns routine tasks into stress tests. The nightclub, on the other hand, is excellent — no complaints there. MC businesses are mostly fine, except the hotbox weed runs, which are more frustrating than fun.

My biggest issues are with the NPCs and traffic AI. Enemies are absurdly accurate and overly tanky, and the traffic behaves like a coordinated hive mind dedicated to sabotaging whatever fun you’re having. After nearly 200 hours, the returns on enjoyment feel sharply diminished — the fun still exists, but it’s increasingly rare, while the stress carries over even after logging off.

I returned to Grand Theft Auto V Enhanced thinking I knew this city by heart.
Los Santos disagreed.

This isn’t a reinvention.
It’s a reminder of how well this world was built in the first place — now sharpened, smoothed, and unapologetically confident.

Everything feels tighter.
Lighting hits harder.
Streets feel denser.
Nighttime finally looks like a place where bad decisions are born.

GTA V was always about contrast.
Sunshine and corruption.
Freedom and consequences.
Three protagonists pulling the same world in different moral directions.

Enhanced doesn’t change that — it amplifies it.

Michael is still trapped by comfort.
Franklin still wants more than the streets will allow.
Trevor is still chaos with a pulse.

What hits harder now is the pacing.
Switching characters feels instant.
Chases flow better.
Gunfights are cleaner, louder, more readable.

The city breathes more.
Crowds react faster.
Traffic feels angrier.
Los Santos doesn’t just exist — it pushes back.

Online content looms in the background, but the single-player experience still stands tall.
The writing hasn’t aged — it’s matured into satire that feels even sharper today.

• I drove aimlessly → the city told stories.
• I followed missions → the characters unraveled.
• I caused chaos → the game smiled and let me.

GTA V Enhanced doesn’t ask you to relearn anything.
It asks you to remember why this worked so well.

It’s still absurd.
Still cynical.
Still confident enough to let you fail loudly.

By the end, Los Santos didn’t feel new.
It felt permanent.

I recommend this game if you have a special interest in farming games or are new to gaming as a hobby. But I didn't like it much. Let me explain why. 
-----
While playing I would have waves of enjoyment and boredom. I would do everything i could do, and then like an in-game week later will unlock a new thing that opens up the world a whole lot more. Having the world open up so often is a really awesome feeling, but it could have better pacing so I'm not bored waiting for the next new thing to get me hooked. I played on keyboard and it was a pretty awful experience control-wise. You gotta like, point vaguely at a direction to interact in that direction, but it's all vibe-based and sometimes just doesnt work at all. I'll be aiming left and my character smacks up. or have my cursor directly on a chest but it opens the chest next to it for no reason. These problems are especially exacerbating to the combat system. At first, the combat was fine for the first 80-90 levels of the Mines as its not taken seriously, the monsters are all cute creatures that hardly hurt you, but the later floors, and also the Skull Cavern you unlock later-- just take themselves too seriously. The combat system was not made for anything difficult to be implemented but the developer did so anyway. Another issue I had was that I wished the role-playing elements were stronger. The game starts out as you making your character. I made the character to be a self-insert, but I had very little control over my character's decisions or how I truly present myself as to the other characters. I want to be a homewrecker and date older gentleman >:). but no, the cast is almost entirely college-aged. Sure, theres like, Harvey, but he suspiciously has quite the baby-face going on. I just feel like I'm not the target demographic for the dating pool. Which is okay, but knowing beforehand how queer this game was I was expecting a lot more diversity (Not just talking about age) like for one, I dont think there's a single Asian in the game. and only one descriptively non-Caucasian dateable character? It's a shame. That's actually not completely true based on technicality, but would require spoilers to explain. This next issue may be a bit of a personal issue as I talked to my friends who have played this game, and while they have had issues, never to the extent of I had. but i had TONS of glitches in my playthrough. My save file got corrupted like 4 times in my 80 hours of playtime. Luckily, the game keeps yesterday's save as backup when-needed, so I never lost too much. It shouldn't have ever happened though, especially more than once.
+++++
To list out some positives: I think the level progression with skills and crafting and new abilities are all very well paced; the game is extremely QoL friendly, one example I'd like to shoutout is that despite normal chests and big chests being completely different items, you can just place a big chest ontop of a normal chest to upgrade it, keeping the inventory. Absolutely stunning thoughtfulness and every game needs to do this.; The mini-games, while being brutal in difficulty, were very fun to play.; Should be expected since it is majority a farming game, but the farming gameplay loop was fun, and trying to make your farm as optimal as possible can strike the fancy of a lot of people. All the characters have pretty distinct personalities, all of them had reasons to love them, and reasons to hate them with their character flaws.

Overall, I found the game to be mid and not for me. Still, I might come back to it someday to try out some of the most popular mod(pack)s to see if that makes the experience any bit more enjoyable for me. But mod support isn't native into Steam so I'm not factoring it into my review. 5.5/10

10/10 The Rhythm Game That Carried Me Through High School

Geometry Dash was legitimately my lifeline back in high school. Whenever the stress of exams, assignments, or just teenage nonsense got too heavy, I’d plug in my headphones, fire up the game, and lose myself for hours. It’s not just a game—it’s therapy with sick beats.

The soundtrack is straight-up phenomenal. Every level has its own personality because of the music—those perfectly synced drops, the build-ups, the moments where the beat just hits right as you nail a tricky section. The immersion is unreal; you stop thinking about everything else and become one with the cube/fly/ship/whatever you’re controlling.

And yeah—it’s brutally tricky. You’re going to die. A lot. But that’s the magic. Every failure teaches you something. You learn the patterns, you memorize timings, you train your fingers and your brain until suddenly that impossible section clicks and you’re screaming “LET’S GOOO” at 2 a.m. It forces you to actually get better through repetition, muscle memory, and pure stubbornness. There’s no hand-holding here—just you vs. the level vs. your own limits.

If you want a game that’s equal parts frustrating and insanely rewarding, with a soundtrack that still slaps years later, Geometry Dash is worth every single rage-quit and every perfect run. Still boot it up to this day. Still top-tier.

Buy it. Suffer. Improve. Vibe. Repeat.

One Thumb Up for Baldur’s Gate 3

TL;DR: Incredible combat and environments. Please stop zooming into my face and asking me to emotionally commit.

Incredible production value, great combat pacing, and beautiful environments, but the game leans too heavily on cinematic storytelling and guided interactions. Exploration feels segmented into Acts rather than discovered organically. Dice rolls lose tension due to constant rerolls, and companions feel more like a curated cast than people in a living world. I respect the ambition, but I miss the systems-first design and emergent gameplay of classic CRPGs.

Pros:
Outstanding production value (voice acting, visuals, environmental detail)
Combat pacing feels tight and satisfying
Encounter design is generally strong
Gorgeous maps and atmospheric locations
Huge amount of content and player choice on paper
Accessible systems make it easy to jump in and experiment
Some story moments genuinely land when they’re allowed to breathe

Cons:
So when you walk into goblin camps, towers, or hostile zones and everyone just… talks to you?
Approval meters for characters(no more party reputation)
Cinematics constantly interrupt gameplay flow
Dice rolls feel bureaucratic rather than dramatic due to Inspiration rerolls
Exploration feels chapter-based (“Acts”) instead of world discovery
Companions feel like a curated ensemble rather than people existing independently in the world and you feel forced to care about their outcomes or situations.
Camp centralization removes consequence and permanence.
Class identity is diluted (everyone can steal, pick locks, sneak, etc.) 
Inspiration is a great idea but it diminishes consequences for poor builds as it just allows you to reroll your dice.
Too much hand-holding in major areas and story beats
Evil zones behave like social hubs instead of hostile territory

Roleplay often gives way to systems-driven romance 

Doing basic heroic Paladin things (helping people, solving problems) somehow translates into party members wanting to sleep with you. It starts to feel less like organic relationships and more like: insert good deed, unlock romance cutscene.

No true custom party creation.

Semi spoiler below :

The game introduces morally complex “evil” factions almost immediately, which feels less like natural world-building and more like thematic onboarding. Instead of discovering complexity over time, you’re handed it upfront, making early encounters feel curated rather than emergent.

Semi-spoiler (design moment that sealed it for me):
Late in Act Two, I told hostile hobgoblins to kill themselves instead of choosing the Paladin “trial by combat” option. These are enemies who were literally eating people earlier in the game. They suddenly acted frightened, and immediately afterward I was visited by the Oathbreaker sequence for being “morally wrong.” That was the moment I put the game down. Not because I embraced evil, but because I chose a faster, pragmatic resolution instead of the cinematically approved one. It felt less like roleplay and more like violating an invisible narrative contract. I wasn’t punished for killing evil, I was punished for not killing evil the right way. Playing as a Paladin in a world that suddenly wanted to run a feelings workshop because the close-up of the hobgoblins trembling in fear.

The game had already established these characters as violent enemies, but then abruptly asked me to empathize with them. When I didn’t, I was treated as morally wrong. That disconnect broke immersion. I wasn’t choosing cruelty, I was following the logic Baldur’s Gate has always used: hostile monsters get dealt with. Being asked to pause and emotionally process that felt forced. By that point, I was already fatigued from always taking the “correct” path, so I started exploring alternate dialogue just to see different outcomes. A little disapproval or approval icon would appear with someones name as if I cared what they thought of my actions anymore.  Clicking the Paladin option and rerolling until it succeeded was the safe route.  I decided against it and the game immediately smites me when choosing the alternative.

Conclusion:
A beautifully crafted RPG with excellent combat and presentation, but one that prioritizes cinematic storytelling and accessibility over emergent systems, consequence, and organic exploration. I’m semi enjoying it, but I often feel like I’m navigating a carefully staged experience rather than discovering a living world. The structure feels guarded and chapter-based, with exploration happening inside curated Acts instead of through true map-driven discovery. There are a lot of invisible rails guiding where you go and how you engage, which makes the world feel impressive to look at, but less alive to explore.



It just feels more like a cinematic Divinity-style(which I actually enjoyed more) experience than a true continuation of classic Baldur’s Gate’s systems-first, exploration-driven design. I’m not sure I’ll finish it. While I respect the ambition, the heavily curated pacing and constant cinematic interruptions make it harder for me to stay engaged long-term.

So if it shows 20 and you have +9 that doesn’t mean you have to roll 11 or above, it means you have to get a critical success 20 even with your modifiers. What an absolute braindead mistake on the part of whoever was responsible for that. 

When I hear words like “freedom of choice” I don’t expect to have literally everything hidden behind a luck based system, the dice roll, when there are LITERAL SKILLS AND PROFICIENCIES THAT MEAN ESSENTIALLY NOTHING BECAUSE OF IT. This should not be the case for dialogue pretty much WHAT SO EVER because it doesn’t matter what background or character or class you picked in dialogue when you can just bs roll your way through any chat option on any character essentially destroying any essence of “immersion” within your character.

Dice roll in combat? That’s fine, makes sense, adds some random to the battlefield, I like it. Dice roll for CERTAIN CHECKS in dialogue, as in ones you don’t have a proficiency in? Sure, would make sense and give you the ability to step out of your characters normal choice of path from time to time. But not everything … this isn’t actually dnd … it’s a video game … not a tabletop game. 

Please … for the love of all that is holy in gaming … for my upteenth review of an rpg game now. STOP TRYING TO REINVENT LOCKPICKING. Bethesda got it right, sorry not sorry. So either go with their idea or here is another idea, actually make the lockpicking tools that already exist in your game do their job. They are skill based tool, not a luck one. Stop trying to make it both by having a resource and then a luck roll. It should only be a luck roll if you do NOT have a lockpick kit. Obviously. Having basically everything decided by luck is so boring. It’s not real choice on behalf of the player because if I want to go do something a certain way, well I better hope I get lucky or I will have to go about it another way that I didn’t want. How fun ….. to be forced to not play the game or my character how I want whenever the game feels like it.

If you have really bad frame dips on really good hardware this is probably why. Go to your documents -> My game -> POE2 -> poe2_production_Config. In there change network mode from auto to predictive.

Dead by Daylight isn’t just a game after 20k hours, it’s a legally binding contract I signed with my soul, and every time I boot it up I know I’m about to be mad, disappointed, and weirdly excited all at once, which honestly might be the most terrifying design choice Behavior ever made.

I have 70hrs+ on PC (EA app), so here's my thoughts.

Positives : 
* Immersion is top-tier. The explosions and atmosphere make you feel like you are in a true battlefield.
* It's very polished. The graphics look amazing, even on lower settings. 
* In-game skins look fairly grounded. No COD Nicki Minaj BS.

Negatives :
* There's constant battlepass pop-ups that are intrusive and annoying.
* The battlepass system is designed with FOMO and manipulation in mind. There's certain events that are way too 
   short to grind them normally, promoting you to spend cash, to speed things up. You played 4 hrs per day, every 
   day for the event but didn't manage to unlock your favorite one-time skin? womp womp, poor you, next time 
   swipe your credit card to 'skip tiers'.
* The weapon grind is horrendous. Reaching mastery soft-cap per weapon requires 1k'ish kills. If you game 
   casually (battledad, non-unemployed, etc), expect MONTHS of grinding, just to master a single weapon.
* Unlocking skins for your favorite gun forces you to grind other guns you may not necessarily like, and as i said, 
   grinding your main gun is a pain in the ass, let alone grinding 2+.
* There's clear Netcode and Hit Registration issues with the game, where you'll die while hiding behind objects.
* Maps are poorly designed. They 're either too small (for BF standards), or the big ones are designed in such a 
   manner that heavily promotes camping with sniper rifles. In other words, lots of times you'll die from someone 
   hiding in the bushes 300m away, and there's not much you can do about it. 
* Last, and worst : the TTK. The freaking TTK! It's frustratingly low. In smaller maps, it feels like COD. If they see 
   you first, they'll hipfire you and bang! You 're dead. Which makes the game more of reflex-based, instead of 
   strategy-based.

Overall : 4.5/10. I would NOT recommend BF6, unless it's on discount AND you play for the immersion.

Seems this is gonna be a controversial take but RedSec can co-exist with the vanilla experience, there are enough studios under the EA and Battlefield Studios umbrella to support both experiences. We can have the classic BF and RedSec experiences as long as it is a stable and fully supported experience for each audience that it is intended for. The issue some seem to be mistaking for resource issues is proper leadership and management as this gets harder given there's practically a team in every timezone working on this game, I can only imagine the difficulty for managing that. 

I believe that the technical debt networking/game engineers have need to be addressed first and foremost as it is a basis across all experiences for the game. Server infrastructure needs to have audits and fixes applied to correct some of the issues that are prevalent. The sysadmin team needs more hands or bigger budget. The game clearly has gameplay bugs that signal underlying game engine issues that need more TLC to make a stable foundation for the systems that rely on it for the other teams to make passes without needing bandaids or spot fixes to unjank the gameplay until the next pass that rejanks the game.

I, quite frankly, don't want bigger for the sake of bigger maps but maps that truly serve the core focus each experience and variety. The community seems to just say bigger maps or better maps but the truth is that maps are not allowed to have identity if they have to fall into specific algorithmic requirements that fatigue the playerbase or then give way to more quickly fall into a gameplay loop that has no way to be broken out of that breaks player engagement over time. I want to be clear, bigger maps will not fix the issue as barren wastelands are just a repeat of past mistakes. Maps need to have a clear overall purpose and ways for each class and their playstyle to work while allowing there to be a clear Rock, Paper, Scissors flow for vehicle/infantry interactions with intermission areas for players to breathe. Does that make maps larger, in some cases it will but there can be a way for maps to have better variety if one map has a greater focus on ground combat and another a bit of combined arms or all-out-warfare. Clarity of who's the invading force and the defending force and the asymmetry that provides gives greater gameplay roles to each team. This would break up the impression of whether you are PAX or NATO, you remove the spawn menu reminder no one would be able to tell who they were.

I will agree with the rest of the community that the promises made for portal haven't been kept and a large reason of which is that I honestly don't care if bot farming exists. Streamlining the server browsing experience and discoverability of portal experiences would fix the impression of the overrunning of bot farms and xp servers.

Progression in this game has two main issues. Career progression is long but ultimately pointless and weapon/class progression is long but gatekeeps the full experience. This is why there are so many bot farms because instead of using every gun or gadget in the game to figure out your playstyle or needs your team needs over the course of a game or play session, you are grinding a weapon for hours or navigating challenges that may or may not track progress correctly, are confusing or require a specific playstyle for longer than a player should have to endure to figure out if they want to do it at all. I've thought about the way that challenges could be optional to leveling up a class linearly or branch out to subclasses so players can unlock what they want to use without making it required to use a gun or gadget on the mountain outskirts of Firestorm they don't like to get the one they want. Career rank should either stay pointless or truly give the player rewards for their time investment.

Leveling weapons for attachments should not be a grind but mastering them should. Leveling a gun up should allow the player to play the strategy game of working out what attachments to adapt it to the situation they up against or picking a better gun for the task without the time investment of months to have said options. 

Battle passes work fine but seasonally gatekeeping them has passed. Many players, myself included, do not have the time to invest for weeks to grind a pass that I should be able to earn the content I paid for at my own pace. Item bundles, shop items, LTMs and events are understandable to support a game but as long as they are not broken, mismanaged or grindfests for subpar or AI generated items. I will pay to support games that support real developers and artists that make content that is real or as promised for the genre and art style of the game I was sold on.

There are games you play, and then there are games you survive. DayZ belongs firmly in the second category. At first glance, it looks like another open-world survival game: zombies, hunger meters, abandoned towns, scattered guns. But anyone who’s spent more than a few hours in Chernarus knows that description barely scratches the surface. DayZ is not about objectives, progression trees, or power fantasies. It’s about existence, endurance, and the quiet, constant tension that everything you have can be taken away in seconds. You spawn with almost nothing and the game asks a single question: “How long can you last?” The answer is never simple. You’ll starve, bleed, drink contaminated water, get sick, and die in ways that feel unfair, but every death teaches you something real. Each respawn is not a setback; it’s an opportunity to apply the knowledge you’ve gained. DayZ doesn’t pretend to be fair; it pretends to be real. That honesty is what makes it extraordinary.

The world of Chernarus is enormous, empty, and beautiful. Fields stretch endlessly, forests swallow entire towns, and buildings sit abandoned, filled with silence and decay. You can walk for twenty minutes without seeing another player, another infected, or any sign of life beyond the environment itself, and yet, you are never truly safe. Every rustling leaf, distant gunshot, or open door keeps you on edge. The infected aren’t the real threat; they are environmental pressure, forcing you to move deliberately, think carefully, and respect your surroundings. One wrong move in a town can get you surrounded, wounded, or killed. And then there are other players. Every human you meet is unpredictable: they might help you, rob you, pretend to be friendly before shooting you in the back. There are no factions, no alignment systems, no scripts to tell you who to trust. This is the human element that defines DayZ. Trust is fragile, betrayal is personal, and even the smallest encounter can become a story you tell for years.

Survival in DayZ is everything. Hunger, thirst, injury, sickness, blood loss, and weight are all intertwined. Food isn’t just a resource; it’s a plan. Water isn’t just a pickup; it’s a risk. Health isn’t just a bar; it’s a fragile, ever-changing state that demands attention. Starvation is slow and cruel, pushing you into risky situations. Drinking untreated water can make you violently sick. Every injury, every bite, every fever changes how you approach the world. Bandages, morphine, rags, and medkits all matter. Stamina affects movement, carrying capacity affects combat, and every decision has weight. There are no shortcuts, no magic buttons, no “convenience mechanics” to smooth over the tension. Every choice is meaningful, and every mistake can spiral into disaster.

Combat is tense and deliberate. Guns feel heavy, aim is slow, reloads are manual, and every shot makes noise that can alert zombies or other players. This isn’t an arcade shooter; it’s a high-stakes simulation where avoiding a fight is often wiser than engaging. Close-quarters encounters are terrifying and chaotic. Melee combat is desperate and personal; one wrong swing can leave you bleeding while your opponent finishes the job. PvP in DayZ is a psychological game as much as a physical one. Players lie, bait, bluff, and manipulate. Voice chat is deadly — a calm tone can disarm suspicion, a laugh can betray a plan, a single word can mean life or death. The choices are complex: kill on sight, cooperate, or take the risk of helping someone and hope they don’t betray you. Every encounter carries weight, and the consequences linger long after death.

Exploration and environmental storytelling are central to DayZ. Chernarus doesn’t hand you its secrets; it asks you to notice them. Road signs, terrain features, power lines, coastlines, and even the sun and stars become navigation tools. Each town tells a story through abandoned cars, stripped hospitals, and barricaded homes. Military zones are tense, high-risk areas that offer powerful loot but can quickly become deathtraps. Weather and night cycles force careful planning. Rain can make you cold and sick, fog reduces visibility, and darkness is genuinely dark, forcing choices between stealth and safety. These systems aren’t just decorative; they make the world feel alive, dangerous, and real.

Base-building and stashes offer temporary safety but nothing is permanent. Logs, nails, and gates take time to collect and construct, and every base carries the risk of being raided. Stashes allow quiet, patient survival, rewarding knowledge and subtlety. Gear attachment is real: after hours of scavenging, you hesitate to risk it all, and losing it is as emotionally impactful as any betrayal. Long-term survival changes how you play — you become cautious, patient, and strategic. DayZ teaches that longevity comes from restraint, not aggression.

DayZ’s imperfections — desync, glitches, janky animations — are part of its character. The game’s origins as a mod, its complex simulation systems, and its persistent world create moments of chaos and unpredictability that feel real. Cars flip, players get stuck, physics misbehaves, and yet when everything works, the game delivers moments no other survival game can: tense standoffs, desperate escapes, unlikely friendships, and stories you will never forget. Community servers, mods, and roleplay expand the possibilities even further, allowing creativity, emergent storytelling, and immersion beyond the base game.

Ultimately, DayZ is about people, stories, and survival. You don’t just play it; you live it. Every death, every betrayal, every unlikely alliance is meaningful. You feel the weight of your choices. You remember every moment of fear, relief, and triumph. DayZ doesn’t promise comfort, convenience, or fairness. It promises possibility. It demands patience, observation, and courage. It teaches humility, resilience, and the value of every life — digital or otherwise. For those who embrace it, DayZ is unforgettable, emotionally powerful, and unlike any other game. You don’t just play DayZ. You survive it. You tell its stories. You remember them. And somehow, no matter how many times you die, you always come back to the coast.

DayZ is not a game that wants you to have fun.
It wants you to survive, and those are two very different things.

You spawn with nothing. No tutorial, no direction, no mercy. You’re hungry, cold, bleeding, and confused—and that’s just the first 10 minutes. Every can of food feels like a miracle. Every bullet matters. Every mistake is permanent.

The atmosphere is where DayZ truly shines. The map is massive, quiet, and unsettling. Long moments of silence are suddenly broken by distant gunshots, footsteps in a building, or a door opening behind you. The tension is constant, and no other game does paranoia this well.

PvP encounters are rare, but when they happen, your heart rate skyrockets. One fight can end hours—or days—of progress. Trusting another player is a gamble, and betrayal is always a real possibility.

DayZ is slow. Very slow. If you’re looking for instant action, this game will punish you with boredom. But if you enjoy immersion, realism, and storytelling through gameplay, DayZ delivers unforgettable moments.

The game still has bugs and jank—animations, physics, random deaths—but somehow, they’ve become part of the experience. Frustrating? Yes. Game-breaking? Not usually.

What makes DayZ special is the stories you create.
A random stranger who saves you.
A long journey that ends in one bad decision.
A firefight you’ll remember for years.

You know, I'm having a great time with this. 

If you play Starfield looking for a spaceflight sim, or a sci-fi shoot-em-up, or Bethesda-Jedi, you will be disappointed; but if you play Starfield as a questing game set in space, you'll probably enjoy it!

Honestly, I think the 'mixed' reviews are partly because of people overhyping themselves on what to expect; it does quite a few different things reasonably well - as a game it's gone for a selection of options to keep you engaged, rather than deep-diving on one particular aspect. 

It plays quite similarly to Fallout 4 in regards to combat, somewhat Skyrim++, but without VATS. I vibe pretty well with that style of combat, but it's not for everyone. That, and you will have to be more proactive to discover quests, tasks, and what-have-yous; space is big, it's easy to miss things. 
My biggest praise is for the worldbuilding and setting. It's a really novel near-future world (worlds?) with some excellent attention to setting detail and history. I'm having a great time learning about the history from 2025 to 2305. 

My biggest disappointment is actually the music and soundscape; whilst most of the music is great (Bethesda usually are ppretty good with their soundtracks), there are a few tracks that are extremely irritating to listen to: discordant, inconsistent in intensity, and enormous ear-worms that refuse to leave my brain. 
So much so I've turned off the music and replaced it with ambient tracks on winamp... which then highlights the noticeable lack of good ambient / environmental sound in busy areas. It seem the music was doing the heavy lifting there. 

The thing they could improve the most? More variety in radiant missions - the ones you get from random little settlements. 

I don't think this game is worth £59.99; don't buy it at that price. £29.99? Sure. Anything less than that, give it a go!

[h1]The biggest issue with having so much cringe aboard an exploratory space craft is that the jokes never land[/h1]

Mass Effect Andromeda had all the hallmarks of a hilarious disaster upon release back in 2017. It was a buggy, disjointed, ugly mess of a game, a production hell behind the scenes, and an amphitheatre of pointing and laughing from its audience. Even before this, it faced a weird legacy challenge; the original trilogy was (and still is) widely adored, meaning it had very large shoes to fill. At the same time, Andromeda needed to rally against the exceptionally poor reception garnered by the lacklustre ending to Mass Effect 3 that had finished the series on a sour note. To combat this, EA gathered the celebrated creative team behind the previous three games and put them right to work. On new IP, Anthem. History has not judged this to have been a good idea. Instead, Andromeda was to be built by an entirely new team. On an entirely new engine. With the scope and direction being changed completely every time someone in a position of leadership was cycled away from the title. Which was shockingly often.

The new engine meant that none of the assets from the previous games could be reused. Everything from entire galaxies, character animations and muzzle flashes needed to be created anew by an unfamiliar team with revolving door management. So, it's of little surprise that what day one buyers got was a game populated by murderous-looking mannequins with lizard lips and legs constructed entirely of kneecaps. Walls became suggestion rather than reality. Stairs were a softly whispered rumour, unascendable monstrosities of broken dreams, the possessive guardians of slightly raised platforms. But the faces, dear reader, the faces have gone down in derpy meme legend. Many were bad, but the truest victim was that of the female default protagonist, who seemed to have been expertly sculpted to scientific imperfection. The unsettling facial tics, the disturbing smoothness and expansive reach of the cheeks and forehead. Eyes that can't help but wander, as if trying to escape the hellscape in which they were trapped. But it was mainly that smile, equal parts predatory and gormless. It haunts my dreams.

Fortunately, the walking nightmare that was Sarah Ryder has since been patched to the point where she's merely just horrific to look at. Structural integrity has been enforced so most walls are no longer constructed of mist. Cut scenes no longer feature suicidal characters holding their guns backwards. It's better, but not perfect. For example! During my playthrough, one member of the crew was so intent on avoiding a conversation that his pathfinding took him into and through a computer embankment, where they stayed until the next time we docked the ship. Another time, upon completing a side mission, an in-game cut scene triggered where the team gathered around their won objective and discussed the next step. Only, the world around them remained active and a pack of ravenous space dogs spawned in and killed everyone while they calmly stood around chatting. I wasn't even mad; ignoring a horrific mauling while casually discussing the mundane transportation of glowy space rocks was pretty funny.

As of right now, the game is as solid as it's ever going to be, its oft-mocked technical flaws relegated to frustrating rather than game breaking. For people like me (Gary Hartley, noted Mass Effect enjoyer) who avoided the game at launch to join in with the pointing and laughing from afar, that reason for abstention isn't nearly as valid. It was brave of me, I know, to wade in to see if there was something hiding there behind the bug wall. In my 100 or so hour odyssey through Andromeda, I still found plenty of things to be disappointed by. But more than my fair share of pleasant surprises.

Let's start on a high. The main idea and mission behind Andromeda are great. Trilogy hero, Shepard, was a Spectre agent who, by design, had all their universe's political weight and resources at their disposal. In contrast, Team Ryder has been bundled aboard an ark ship, frozen for 600 years and transported an entire galaxy away. There's no safety net; there's no resources or help at all, and anything they need they're going to have to scourge up themselves from a collection of unexplored systems. The only upshot is that before they left the Milky Way behind, they'd managed to earmark several golden planets, ripe for habitation. That was a lie. Instead, they find inhospitable death worlds filled with unbreathable air, intolerable atmospheres and homicidal local wildlife. The first plant you visit is a disaster; crash landings, scattered crewmates, heavy background radiation and rock-faced xenophobic aliens trying to gun everyone down. It's far from the shiny new home the expedition promised. There was also supposed to be a huge hub ship constructed by the time you arrived, something akin to a smaller scale citadel from the original trilogy. It exists, but it's bare bones. Half constructed, low on power and short staffed. Many people died during the construction, many more abandoned the project, exiling themselves, gambling on having better luck on the scattershot planets that are only nearly inhabitable. More still stay cytogenetically frozen; the way things are, there's not enough resources available to justify thawing them.

Your first real mission is supposed to change that. There's a nearby planet that would merely be a horrific place to live if not for the absence of water and sweltering non-stop desert heat. There's been two previous attempts to establish a settlement, both of which have led to the death of many prospectors. The few survivors returned so damaged and shell-shocked, they were placed back on ice. It's a suicide mission by any optic, but it's also the best part of the game. Failure means everyone dies, so you need to brute force yourself through the endless obstacles your would-be hellfire home presents. At this point, all that really awaits you is various shades of failure. You're under levelled; you're under equipped and if you stray outside the heatproof barrier set up inside the now dead settlements, you'll fry on the spot. Also, those barriers, the only thing keeping you alive, are all failing. There are scavengers picking the bones of the sites; To Shepard, this would be a minor inconvenience, one easily bullied, manipulated or shot into compliance. Ryder can do none of these things; they can only appeal to the scavenger's humanity and shared interest in the newest expedition's success. But this does net new resources. A small victory, but one that gives you more options, the ability to push a little further into the planet. It's the Wild West out there; unexplored desert plains filled with unforeseeable dangers. Lost alien artifacts, acid-spitting sand bugs, rolling metal-melting heatwaves and rock-faced alien arseholes with laser rifles.

You can't do much, but you can do something. So, you scrape. And you scramble. You find little pockets of progression and each small win makes the world of difference. As the planet is slowly tamed, as your foothold in this new galaxy becomes firmer, things change in your favour. You find ways to make the planet more hospitable; you find ways to drive hostile forces out; you find the means to establish a new settlement. With the means to support more life, more people are defrosted at the hub; new areas on the ship are opened and become explorable. Old departments are expanded, looking into newly discovered life and flora and geography. And you've done this. You've explored the unknown and you've been directly responsible for every advancement. You've seen it grow in real time. It's as exhilarating as it is short lived; none of it is present for the remaining five planets.

I've played through the original trilogy at least six times now... And after recently playing through it again I figured I should give Andromeda another chance. I've seen many people say that it has gotten much better since launch and while the story isn't so great compared to the trilogy, the combat supposedly is the best...

I disagree, vehemently. 

My main gripe is, it's just not a mass effect game imho. The combat is very different and I guess people that say it's better just prefer a different style of game. The biggest change is that the power wheel is gone. You can't pause combat anymore to look around, command your teammates and choose your powers. Instead it's all real-time and you can only have three powers on your bumpers (one of which by hitting them together). As far as I've been able to see you can't command your teammates to use powers... Actually in the time I've played I don't think I've seen anything to indicate that they have any at all, it's just that I've seen there is an achievement to combo with them so they must. But there is no more tactical looking around and combining powers. 

The shooting seems pretty good, but not really anything special. One other thing that annoys... They still have the weight system to hurt your cooldowns if you carry too many weapons. I started as an infiltrator (it's called differently now, operative maybe)... But if I take a sniper with me my cooldowns immediately are shot. So I end up bringing an assault rifle because with the sniper I can't use my cloak very often. This can be fixed later with skill points, but it kind of kills the class at the start. 

Graphics are pretty cool, as long as you don't look too closely at the faces (especially the Rider men look like they got a skin condition).

Controls are a bit weird and coming from ME LE it's annoying they changed everything and you can't customise the controls (not on a controller anyway). One thing that really frustrated me is that x is reload, but holding x is swap weapons and that seems to be glitchy where it triggers a lot even though I was not holding the button down. I have had so many times where I was suddenly shooting the damn pistol instead of my AR... Also pressing B is dodge, which is pretty cool... But you can't manually go into cover anymore, you just have to kind of walk into cover while having your weapon out. And if you press B you just blink forward, which has made me jump off a cliff several times. Maybe it's partly me but even after playing for 6 hours I still find the controls overly complicated and unintuitive. 

The story so far is pretty uninteresting, but this was expected, no-one praises Andromeda for its story. 

The worst part though, coming back to that this is not a Mass Effect game... They could have dropped Mass Effect from the name, changed the names of some skills and weapons, changed the models of some aliens to humans and you wouldn't have been able to tell it was supposed to be a mass effect game. Yes there are Asari, Krogan, Salarian and Turian, but they act just like humans. There is no difference, the only thing they took from Mass Effect is how they look. 

So in the end this is just a generic scifi shooter with rpg elements... It's not bad per se, but there are so many much better games, that I just can't recommend anyone wastes their time on this.

It’s honestly hard for me to review this game because I started playing it right after finishing the Mass Effect trilogy. I was still emotionally attached to the characters and the whole universe and didn’t want it to end, like an addict taking a weaker drug just to slowly come off the stronger one.

The graphics are beautiful, and the gameplay is solid. There are multiple class/playstyle variations again, but system is more flexible, you’re not locked into one class and can switch profiles depending on your skills.
I do have to say the game felt a bit bloated in terms of exploration and missions. There’s a lot of filler content. Personally, I didn’t mind it too much and ended up completing everything, but I know other people found it repetitive. The game also has several easter eggs connecting it to the original trilogy, references to the Milky Way, mentions of Shepard as a legendary figure, audio logs hinting at Liara work as an information broker, Krogan settling on a New Tuchanka, and familiar N7 gear.

As for the story… I’ll be honest, the new Angara race didn’t fully click with me. Something about them felt a bit off, and the whole plot sometimes came across more like a side story rather than a strong main narrative driving the universe forward. The dialogue also lacked the weight and emotional punch of the original Mass Effect games. It felt a bit flat at times. And don't get me started on Liam... he’s the one character I genuinely avoided talking to whenever possible. I don’t think I’ve seen a more poorly written character in the series. It almost felt like a self insert by a developer or something because of how annoying he was. The storyline involving the Jardaan, the Remnant, and the Kett felt somewhat unfinished, becuase they teased a sequel, but since that clearly not happening, the overall narrative ends up feeling a bit underwhelming.

The game isn’t bad by any means. If you enjoyed the Mass Effect trilogy or sci-fi exploration games in general, you’ll probably have a good time here too. Just don’t expect the same level of storytelling, character depth, and emotional impact as the original trilogy.

Despite the common complaints concerning performance issues, my game only crashed twice during my entire playtime. I played on GeForce Now, so I believe if played with a sufficiently powerful computer such issues are not relevant. Just thought I should put that out there in case its useful. 

Now, the actual game itself. 10/10. This is what a Star Wars game should be. Having played and loved Jedi Fallen Order/Survivor, I was initially hesitant to approach this game, since I wasn't too excited about the idea of playing as an average "outlaw" as opposed to a Jedi. BUT, I was 100% WRONG! The experience of playing this game, is as "Star Wars" as it gets. The amount of love put in by all of the development team is absurd. The detail to attention, the cameos/references, the world building. Everything is true to the soul of Star Wars and builds on it masterfully. The music is memorable and fitting, at times with clear motifs from John Williams' scores. The sounds, graphics, combat. Everything feels really immersive and natural. The story feels simple, yet there is depth to the character(s). The main character (Kay Vess) has a sidekick pet (Nix) and it's amazing how they've managed to build so much functionality into him. For the first time playing a game, I felt like the "pet" was not just decorative but actually part of the experience. That brings me to level design. The level design is also brilliant. It is obvious, clear, there is a good bit of challenging combat, and ease of navigation (especially with climbing which is actually fast and not frustratingly slow). The amount of diverse aliens, languages, enemies, worlds, environments, lighting is really immersive in the vast universe of Star Wars. Playing is satisfying, stealth is actually rewarding and not frustrating or boring. The side quests are nuanced. There is also a lot of dynamic interactions in the game: dialogues adapt based on the actions/decisions/quests you do. The story and relationships are also nuanced and doesn't just feel like a boring or repetitive story. 

This is a really fun, impressive, and original game--all the while being a STAR WARS game. It is sad this game hasn't been optimized to be playable for the more general consumer. If I had played this on my own gaming computer, I am sure I would have had a very different view. As I said, I was running it on GeForce Now with MAXXED out settings on a 5080RTX card, and it was running at around 10-12 GB of VRAM. If you have a very capable machine, or are able to play through cloud gaming, I would very much recommend this game. Oh I also got it for $20 bucks discounted so that's pretty sweet. Anyways, I hope this was helpful.
